 His ‘Gray Divorce’ at 67 Should Be Final by Dec. 31. If It Slips to January and He Files Separately, $30,600 of His $36,000 in Social Security Becomes Taxable Instead of $7,900
 Gerelyn Terzo Wed, November 18, 2026 at 8:02 PM CST 5 min read Quick Read 
 A divorce decree dated by December 31 makes him single for all of 2026, while a January decree leaves him married for tax purposes. 
 Filing separately after a January decree removes the Social Security shield, taxing $30,600 of his benefits instead of $7,900 and costing about $3,400 in total. 
 He can limit the damage by pushing for a December hearing or running a joint return, though joint filing makes both spouses liable for the tax.

 A 67-year-old man has spent most of 2026 dissolving a marriage. The settlement is signed, the house is listed, and his lawyer expects the final decree before Christmas. Social Security pays him $36,000 a year, and his pension adds $20,000. If the judge's signature slips even a week into January, his 2026 tax bill changes in a way few people see coming. 
 24/7 Wall St. He has plenty of company. Divorces among spouses 50 and older, otherwise known as "gray divorces," have roughly doubled since 1990 and now make up nearly 40% of U.S. divorces, according to a New York Times analysis. For those couples, a court calendar can decide how much of their Social Security gets taxed. 
 One Signature Date Decides His Filing Status for All of 2026 
 The IRS looks at a single day. If you are divorced under a final decree by the last day of the year, you are considered unmarried for the whole year. If the divorce is still pending on December 31, you are treated as married for all of 2026, even if you moved out in March.

 Filing status matters here because of how benefits factor into taxable income. The IRS adds your other income to half your Social Security to get a figure often called combined income. For him, that is $20,000 of pension plus $18,000 (half his benefits), or $38,000. 
 Why a January Decree Makes Nearly Every Benefit Dollar Taxable 
 As a single filer, his first $25,000 of combined income shields his benefits completely. Over the next $9,000, up to $34,000, half of each dollar counts. Above that, 85% counts. 
 Story Continues His result: $4,500 from the middle band plus 85% of the $4,000 above the top line, for $7,900 of taxable benefits. 
 Now picture the decree landing January 6. He is still married for 2026, and few divorcing spouses want to sign a joint return together. A separate filer who lived with a spouse at any time during the year faces a base amount of $0. No shielded band exists. The worksheet simply taxes 85% of his benefits, or $30,600. 
 A one-week delay adds $22,700 of taxable income. At the 12% rate covering most of it, his federal tax rises by about $2,700. 
 A second hit follows. The new $6,000 senior deduction for people 65 and older is available to a married person only if the couple files a joint return. 
 Losing it costs him about $720 more at 12%, bringing the total damage near $3,400. 
 How His Pension Turns Into a Lever Against Him 
 His pension is fully taxable under either status, so its real role is leverage. As a single filer, the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 plus the senior deduction keeps most of his income in the lowest bracket. Filing separately, that same pension drags almost every Social Security dollar into taxable territory. 
 A joint return is the escape hatch, since the joint base amount is $32,000. The catch: his spouse's income gets added to his, and both spouses may be held responsible, jointly and individually for the tax on that return, even after the divorce. That is a hard conversation mid-settlement. 
 One narrow exception exists. A married person filing separately who lived apart from the spouse for all of 2026 keeps the $25,000 base amount. If they shared a home even in January, that door is already closed. 
 Two Moves Worth Making Before New Year's Eve 
 First, give your divorce attorney the tax stakes in dollars. Courts and opposing counsel respond to details, and "a January signature costs me about $3,400" is a concrete reason to push for a December hearing. Your former spouse may face a similar penalty, which gives both sides a shared reason to finish on time. 
 Second, if the date slips anyway, have a preparer run the 2026 return both ways before filing. A joint return coupled with written terms in the settlement about who pays the tax may leave both of you ahead of two separate returns. The IRS sets your filing status by the decree date alone, and missing that is the mistake hardest to undo. 
 State law decides exactly when a decree becomes final, and every divorce file has its own complications, so a short call with a tax professional in December can save far more than it costs. This filing-status trap is one of several IRS rules that silently drain retirement accounts, and we mapped the rest in a free guide here: The Retiree's Tax Trap Map.
